entries.e4cacab6eb30c0d465e40a78b5dee3320baeb161: <div sID="gen16540" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="46" osisID="Isa.46" sID="Isa.46"/> <div eID="gen16540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16541" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16542" type="x-p"/> God, by the prophet here, designing shortly to deliver them out of their captivity, prepared them for that deliverance by possessing them with a detestation of idols and with a believing confidence in God, even their own God. I. Let them not be afraid of the idols of Babylon, as if they could in any way obstruct their deliverance, for they should be defaced (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.1-Isa.46.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>); but let them trust in that God who had often delivered them to do it still, to do it now, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.3-Isa.46.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. II. Let them not think to make idols of their own, images of the God of Israel, by them to worship him, as the Babylonians worship their gods, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.5-Isa.46.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. Let them not be so sottish (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.8">ver. 8</reference>), but have an eye to God in his word, not in an image; let them depend upon that, and upon the promises and predictions of it, and God's power to accomplish them all, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.9-Isa.46.11">ver. 9-11</reference>. And let them know that the unbelief of man shall not make the word of God of no effect, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.12-Isa.46.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>.
entries.c22bdd1f3816f4aac74cdb9660bfa04921236f6d: <div eID="gen16542" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16541" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Folly of Idolatry. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 708.)</title> <div sID="gen16543" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Bel boweth down, Nebo stoopeth, their idols were upon the beasts, and upon the cattle: your carriages <hi type="italic">were</hi> heavy loaden; <hi type="italic">they are</hi> a burden to the weary <hi type="italic">beast.</hi> <hi type="super">2</hi> They stoop, they bow down together; they could not deliver the burden, but themselves are gone into captivity. <hi type="super">3</hi> Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, which are borne <hi type="italic">by me</hi> from the belly, which are carried from the womb: <hi type="super">4</hi> And <hi type="italic">even</hi> to <hi type="italic">your</hi> old age I <hi type="italic">am</hi> he; and <hi type="italic">even</hi> to hoar hairs will I carry <hi type="italic">you:</hi> I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver <hi type="italic">you.</hi> <div eID="gen16543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16544" type="x-p"/> We are here told, <div eID="gen16544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16545" type="x-p"/> I. That the false gods will certainly fail their worshippers when they have most need of them, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.1-Isa.46.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Bel and Nebo were two celebrated idols of Babylon. Some make Bel to be a contraction of Baal; others rather think not, but that it was Belus, one of their first kings, who after his death was deified. As Bel was a deified prince, so (some think) Nebo was a deified prophet, for so Nebo signifies; so that Bel and Nebo were their Jupiter and their Mercury or Apollo. Barnabas and Paul passed at Lystra for Jupiter and Mercury. The names of these idols were taken into the names of their princes, Bel into Belshazzar's, Nebo into Nebuchadnezzar's and Nebuzaradan's, &c. These gods they had long worshipped, and in their revels praised them for their successes (as appears, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.4">Dan. v. 4</reference>); and they insulted over Israel as if Bel and Nebo were too hard for Jehovah and could detain them in captivity in defiance of their God. Now, that this might be no discouragement to the poor captives, God here tells them what shall become of these idols, which they threaten them with. When Cyrus takes Babylon, down go the idols. It was usual then with conquerors to destroy the gods of the places and people they conquered, and to put the gods of their own nation in the room of them, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.19">ch. xxxvii. 19</reference>. Cyrus will do so; and then Bel and Nebo, that were set up on high, and looked great, bold, and erect, shall <hi type="italic">stoop and bow down</hi> at the feet of the soldiers that plunder their temples. And because there is a great deal of gold and silver upon them, which was intended to adorn them, but serves to expose them, they carry them away with the rest of the spoil. The carriers' horses, or mules, are laden with them and their other idols, to be sent among other lumber (for so it seems they accounted them rather than treasure) into Persia. So far are they from being able to support their worshippers that they are themselves a heavy load in the wagons, and <hi type="italic">a burden to the weary beast.</hi> The idols cannot help one another (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">They stoop, they bow down together.</hi> They are all alike, tottering things, and their day has come to fall. Their worshippers cannot help them: <hi type="italic">They could not deliver the burden</hi> out of the enemy's hand, <hi type="italic">but themselves</hi> (both the idols and the idolaters) <hi type="italic">have gone into captivity.</hi> Let not therefore God's people be afraid of either. When God's ark was taken prisoner by the Philistines it proved a burden, not to the beasts, but to the conquerors, who were forced to return it; but, when Bel and Nebo have gone into captivity, their worshippers may even give their good word with them: they will never recover themselves. <div eID="gen16545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16546" type="x-p"/> II. That the true God will never fail his worshippers: "You hear what has become of Bel and Nebo, now <hi type="italic">hearken to me, O house of Jacob!</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.46.3-Isa.46.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. Am I such a god as these? No; though you are brought low, and the house of Israel is but a remnant, your God has been, is, and ever will be, your powerful and faithful protector." <div eID="gen16546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16547" type="x-p"/> 1. Let God's Israel do him the justice to own that he has hitherto been kind to them, careful of them, tender over them, and has all along done well for them. Let them own, (1.) That he bore them at first: <hi type="italic">I have made.</hi> Out of what womb came they, but that of his mercy, and grace, and promise? He formed them into a people and gave them their constitution. Every good man is what God makes him. (2.) That he bore them up all along: You have been <hi type="italic">borne by me from the belly,</hi> and <hi type="italic">carried from the womb.</hi> God began betimes to do them good, as soon as ever they were formed into a nation, nay, when as yet they were very few, and strangers. God took them under a special protection, and <hi type="italic">suffered no man to do them wrong,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.105.12-Ps.105.14">Ps. cv. 12-14</reference>. In the infancy of their state, when they were not only foolish and helpless, as children, but forward and peevish, God carried them in the arms of his power and love, bore them <hi type="italic">as upon eagles' wings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.19.4">Exod. xix. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">Deut. xxxii. 11</reference>. Moses had not patience <hi type="italic">to carry them as the nursing father does the sucking child</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.11.12">Num. xi. 12</reference>), but God bore them, and <hi type="italic">bore their manners,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.18">Acts xiii. 18</reference>. And as God began early to do them good (when <hi type="italic">Israel was a child, then I loved him</hi>), so he had constantly continued to do them good: he had carried them from the womb to this day. And we may all witness for God that he has been thus gracious to us. We have been borne by him from the belly, from the womb, else we should have died from the womb and given up the ghost when we came out of the belly. We have been the constant care of his kind providence, carried in the arms of his power and in the bosom of his love and pity. The new man is so; all that in us which is born of God is borne up by him, else it would soon fail. Our spiritual life is sustained by his grace as necessarily and constantly as our natural life by his providence. The saints have acknowledged that God has carried them from the womb, and have encouraged themselves with the consideration of it in their greatest straits, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.9-Ps.22.10">Ps. xxii. 9, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.71.5-Ps.71.6 Ps.71.17">lxxi. 5, 6, 17</reference>. <div eID="gen16547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16548" type="x-p"/> 2. He will then do them the kindness to promise that he will never leave them. He that was their first will be their last; he that was the author will be the finisher of their well-being (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.4">v. 4</reference>): "You have been <hi type="italic">borne by me from the belly,</hi> nursed when you were children; and <hi type="italic">even to your old age I am he,</hi> when, by reason of your decays and infirmities, you will need help as much as in your infancy." Israel were now growing old, so was their covenant by which they were incorporated, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.13">Heb. viii. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">Gray hairs were here and there upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.7.9">Hos. vii. 9</reference>. And they had hastened their old age, and the calamities of it, by their irregularities. But God will not cast them off now, will not fail them when their strength fails; he is still their God, will still carry them in the same everlasting arms that were laid under them in Moses's time, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.27">Deut. xxxiii. 27</reference>. He has made them and owns his interest in them, and therefore he will bear them, will bear with their infirmities, and bear them up under their afflictions: "Even <hi type="italic">I will carry and will deliver</hi> them; I will now bear them upon eagles' wings out of Babylon, as in their infancy I bore them out of Egypt." This promise to aged Israel is applicable to every aged Israelite. God has graciously engaged to support and comfort his faithful servants, even in their old age: "<hi type="italic">Even to your old age,</hi> when you grow unfit for business, when you are compassed with infirmities, and perhaps your relations begin to grow weary of you, yet <hi type="italic">I am he</hi>—he that I am, he that I have been—the very same by whom you have been borne from the belly and carried from the womb. You change, but I am the same. I am he that I have promised to be, he that you have found me, and he that you would have me to be. <hi type="italic">I will carry you, I will bear,</hi> will bear you up and bear you out, and will carry you on in your way and carry you home at last."
entries.40a6f457f41c1e7d37867328be59284abb6d956c: <div eID="gen16548" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Folly of Idolatry; The Divine Prerogative Asserted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 708.)</title> <div sID="gen16549" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> To whom will ye liken me, and make <hi type="italic">me</hi> equal, and compare me, that we may be like? <hi type="super">6</hi> They lavish gold out of the bag, and weigh silver in the balance, <hi type="italic">and</hi> hire a goldsmith; and he maketh it a god: they fall down, yea, they worship. <hi type="super">7</hi> They bear him upon the shoulder, they carry him, and set him in his place, and he standeth; from his place shall he not remove: yea, <hi type="italic">one</hi> shall cry unto him, yet can he not answer, nor save him out of his trouble. <hi type="super">8</hi> Remember this, and show yourselves men: bring <hi type="italic">it</hi> again to mind, O ye transgressors. <hi type="super">9</hi> Remember the former things of old: for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> God, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none else; <hi type="italic">I am</hi> God, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none like me, <hi type="super">10</hi> Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times <hi type="italic">the things</hi> that are not <hi type="italic">yet</hi> done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure: <hi type="super">11</hi> Calling a ravenous bird from the east, the man that executeth my counsel from a far country: yea, I have spoken <hi type="italic">it,</hi> I will also bring it to pass; I have purposed <hi type="italic">it,</hi> I will also do it. <hi type="super">12</hi> Hearken unto me, ye stouthearted, that <hi type="italic">are</hi> far from righteousness: <hi type="super">13</hi> I bring near my righteousness; it shall not be far off, and my salvation shall not tarry: and I will place salvation in Zion for Israel my glory. <div eID="gen16549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16550" type="x-p"/> The deliverance of Israel by the destruction of Babylon (the general subject of all these chapters) is here insisted upon, and again promised, for the conviction both of idolaters who set up as rivals with God, and of oppressors who were enemies to the people of God. <div eID="gen16550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16551" type="x-p"/> I. For the conviction of those who made and worshipped idols, especially those of Israel who did so, who would have images of their God, as the Babylonians had of theirs, <div eID="gen16551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16552" type="x-p"/> 1. He challenges them either to frame an image that should be thought a resemblance of him or to set up any being that should stand in competition with him (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">To whom will you liken me?</hi> It is absurd to think of representing an infinite and eternal Spirit by the figure of any creature whatsoever. It is to change his truth into a lie and to turn his glory into shame. None ever saw any similitude of him, nor can see his face and live. <hi type="italic">To whom then can we liken God?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.18">ch. xl. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.25">25</reference>. It is likewise absurd to think of making any creature equal with the Creator, who is infinitely above the noblest creatures, yea, or to make any comparison between the creature and the Creator, since between infinite and finite there is no proportion. <div eID="gen16552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16553" type="x-p"/> 2. He exposes the folly of those who made idols and then prayed to them, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.6-Isa.46.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. (1.) They were at great charge upon their idols and spared no cost to fit them for their purpose: <hi type="italic">They lavish gold out of the bag;</hi> no little will serve, and they do not care how much goes, though they pinch their families and weaken their estates by it. How does the profuseness of idolaters shame the niggardliness of many who call themselves God's servants but are for a religion that will cost them nothing! Some <hi type="italic">lavish gold out of the bag</hi> to make an idol of it in the house, while others <hi type="italic">hoard up gold in the bag</hi> to make an idol of it in the heart; for <hi type="italic">covetousness is idolatry,</hi> as dangerous, though not as scandalous, as the other. <hi type="italic">They weigh silver in the balance,</hi> either to be the matter of their idol (for even those that were most sottish had so much sense as to think that God should be served with the best they had, the best they could possibly afford; those that represented him by a calf made it a golden one) or to pay the workmen's wages. The service of sin often proves very expensive. (2.) They were in great care about their idols and took no little pains about them (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">They bear him upon their</hi> own <hi type="italic">shoulders,</hi> and do not hire porters to do it; they <hi type="italic">carry him, and set him in his place,</hi> more like a dead corpse than a living God. They set him on a pedestal, <hi type="italic">and he stands.</hi> They take a great deal of pains to fasten him, and <hi type="italic">from his place he shall not remove,</hi> that they may know where to find him, though at the same time they know he can neither move a hand nor stir a step to do them any kindness. (3.) After all, they paid great respect to their idols, though they were but the works of their own hands and the creatures of their own fancies. When the goldsmith has made it that which they please to call a god <hi type="italic">they fall down, yea, they worship it.</hi> If they magnified themselves too much in pretending to make a god, as if they would atone for that, they vilified themselves as much in prostrating themselves to a god that they knew the original of. And, if they were deceived by the custom of their country in making such gods as these, they did no less deceive themselves when they cried unto them, though they knew they could not answer them, could not understand what they said to them, nor so much as reply Yea, or No, much less could they <hi type="italic">save them out of their trouble.</hi> Now shall any that have some knowledge of, and interest in, the true and living God, thus make fools of themselves? <div eID="gen16553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16554" type="x-p"/> 3. He puts it to themselves, and their own reason, let that judge in the case (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Remember this,</hi> that has been often told you, what senseless helpless things idols are, <hi type="italic">and show yourselves men</hi>—men and not brutes, men and not babes. Act with reason; act with resolution; act for your own interest. Do a wise thing; do a brave thing; and scorn to disparage your own judgment as you do when you worship idols." Note, Sinners would become saints if they would but show themselves men, if they would but support the dignity of their nature and use aright its powers and capacities. "Many things you have been reminded of; <hi type="italic">bring them again to mind,</hi> recall them into you memories, and revolve them there. <hi type="italic">O! you transgressors, consider your ways; remember whence you have fallen, and repent,</hi> and so recover yourselves." <div eID="gen16554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16555" type="x-p"/> 4. He again produces incontestable proofs that he is God, that he and none besides is so (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am God, and there is none like me.</hi> This is that which we have need to be reminded of again and again; for proof of it he refers, (1.) To the sacred history: "<hi type="italic">Remember the former things of old,</hi> what the God of Israel did for his people in their beginnings, whether he did not that for them which no one else could, and which the false gods did not, nor could do, for their worshippers. Remember those things, and you will own that <hi type="italic">I am God and there is none else.</hi>" This is a good reason why we should give glory to him as a nonsuch, and why we should not give that glory to any other which is due to him alone, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Exod. xv. 11</reference>. (2.) To the sacred prophecy. He is God alone, for it is he only that <hi type="italic">declares the end from the beginning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.46.10">v. 10</reference>. From the beginning of time he declared the end of time, and end of all things. Enoch prophesied, <hi type="italic">Behold, the Lord comes.</hi> From the beginning of a nation he declares what the end of it will be. He told Israel what should befal them in <hi type="italic">the latter days,</hi> what <hi type="italic">their end should be,</hi> and wished they were so wise as to consider it, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.20">Deut. xxxii. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.29">29</reference>. From the beginning of an event he declares what the end of it will be. <hi type="italic">Known unto God are all his works,</hi> and, when he pleases, he makes them known. Further than prophecy guides us it is impossible for us to <hi type="italic">find out the work that God makes from the beginning to the end,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.11">Eccl. iii. 11</reference>. He <hi type="italic">declares from ancient times the things that are not yet done.</hi> Many scripture prophecies which were delivered long ago are not yet accomplished; but the accomplishment of some in the mean time is an earnest of the accomplishment of the rest in due time. By this it appears that he is <hi type="italic">God, and none else;</hi> it is he, and none besides, that can say, and make his words good, "<hi type="italic">My counsel shall stand,</hi> and all the powers of hell and earth cannot control or disannul it nor all their policies correct or countermine it." As God's operations are all according to his counsels, so his counsels shall all be fulfilled in his operations, and none of his measures shall be broken, none of his designs shall miscarry. This yields abundant satisfaction to those who have bound up all their comforts in God's counsels, that his counsel shall undoubtedly stand; and, if we are brought to this, that whatever pleases God pleases us, nothing can contribute more to make us easy than to be assured of this, that <hi type="italic">God will do all his pleasure,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.135.6">Ps. cxxxv. 6</reference>. The accomplishment of this particular prophecy, which relates to the elevation of Cyrus and his agency in the deliverance of God's people out of their captivity, is mentioned for the confirmation of this truth, that the Lord is God and there is none else; and this is a thing which shall shortly come to pass, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.11">v. 11</reference>. God by his counsel <hi type="italic">calls a ravenous bird from the east,</hi> a bird of prey, <hi type="italic">Cyrus,</hi> who (they say) had a nose like the beak of a hawk or eagle, to which some think this alludes, or (as others say) to the eagle which was his standard, as it was afterwards that of the Romans, to which there is supposed to be a reference, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.28">Matt. xxiv. 28</reference>. Cyrus came from the east at God's call: for God is Lord of hosts and of those that have hosts at command. And, if God give him a call, he will give him success. He is the man that shall <hi type="italic">execute God's counsel,</hi> though he comes <hi type="italic">from a far country</hi> and knows nothing of the matter. Note, Even those that know not, and mind not, God's revealed will, are made use of to fulfil the counsels of his secret will, which shall all be punctually accomplished in their season by what hand he pleases. That which is here added, to ratify this particular prediction, may abundantly show to the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel: "<hi type="italic">I have spoken of it</hi> by my servants the prophets, and what I have spoken is just the same with what <hi type="italic">I have purposed.</hi>" For, though God has many things in his purposes which are not in his prophecies, he has nothing in his prophecies but what are in his purposes. And he <hi type="italic">will do it,</hi> for he will never change his mind; he <hi type="italic">will bring it to pass,</hi> for it is not in the power of any creature to control him. Observe with what majesty he says it, as one having authority: <hi type="italic">I have spoken it, I will also bring it to pass. Dictum, factum—no sooner said than done. I have purposed it,</hi> and he does not say, "I will take care it shall be done," but, "<hi type="italic">I will do it.</hi>" Heaven and earth shall pass away sooner than one tittle of the word of God. <div eID="gen16555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16556" type="x-p"/> II. For the conviction of those that daringly opposed the counsels of God assurance is here given not only that they shall be accomplished, but that they shall be accomplished very shortly, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.12-Isa.46.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. <div eID="gen16556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16557" type="x-p"/> 1. This is addressed to the <hi type="italic">stout-hearted,</hi> that is, either, (1.) The proud and obstinate Babylonians, <hi type="italic">that are far from righteousness,</hi> far from doing justice or showing mercy to those they have power over, that say they will never let the oppressed go free, but will still detain them in spite of their petitions or God's predictions, that are far from any thing of clemency or compassion to the miserable. Or, (2.) The unhumbled Jews, that have been long under the hammer, long in the furnace, but are not broken are not melted, that, like the unbelieving murmuring Israelites in the wilderness, think themselves far from God's righteousness (that is, from the performance of his promise, and his appearing to judge for them), and by their distrusts set themselves at a yet further distance from it, and keep good things from themselves, as their fathers, who could not enter into the land of promise because of unbelief. This is applicable to the Jewish nation when they rejected the gospel of Christ; though they <hi type="italic">followed after the law of righteousness,</hi> they <hi type="italic">attained not to righteousness, because they sought it not by faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.9.31-Rom.9.32">Rom. ix. 31, 32</reference>. They perished far from righteousness; and it was because they were <hi type="italic">stout-hearted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">Rom. x. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen16557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16558" type="x-p"/> 2. Now to them God says that, whatever they think, the one in presumption, the other in despair, (1.) Salvation shall be certainly wrought for God's people. If men will not do them justice, God will, and his righteousness shall effect that for them which men's righteousness would not reach to. He <hi type="italic">will place salvation in Zion,</hi> that is, he will make Jerusalem a place of safety and defence to all those who will plant themselves there; thence shall salvation go forth <hi type="italic">for Israel his glory.</hi> God glories in his Israel; and he will be glorified in the salvation he designs to work out for them; it shall redound greatly to his honour. This salvation shall be in Zion; for thence the gospel shall take rise (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">ch. ii. 3</reference>), thither the Redeemer comes (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.20">ch. lix. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Rom. xi. 26</reference>), and it is Zion's King that has salvation, <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zech. ix. 9</reference>. (2.) It shall be very shortly wrought. This is especially insisted on with those who thought it at a distance: "<hi type="italic">I bring near my righteousness,</hi> nearer than you think of; perhaps it is nearest of all when your straits are greatest and your enemies most injurious; it shall not be far off when there is occasion for it, <reference osisRef="Ps.85.9">Ps. lxxxv. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Behold, the Judge stands before the door.</hi> My salvation shall not tarry any longer than till it is ripe and you are ready for it; and therefore, <hi type="italic">though it tarry, wait for it;</hi> wait patiently, for <hi type="italic">he that shall come will come, and will not tarry.</hi>"  <chapter eID="Isa.46"/> <div eID="gen16558" type="x-p"/>

entries.f7fd9dc0962bbc67f192a89135accc631fe10443: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9213"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 46</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.46.1-Isa.46.13">Is 46:1-13</reference>. Babylon's Idols Could Not Save Themselves, Much Less Her. But God Can and Will Save Israel: Cyrus Is His Instrument.</title> <div sID="gen15710" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9213"/><hi type="bold">1. Bel--</hi>the same as the Phoenician Baal, that is, lord, the chief god of Babylon; to it was dedicated the celebrated tower of Babylon, in the center of one of the two parts into which the city was divided, the palace being in the center of the other. Identical with the sun, worshipped on turrets, housetops, and other high places, so as to be nearer the heavenly hosts (Saba) (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.13">Jr 19:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.29">32:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.1.5">Zep 1:5</reference>). Gesenius identifies Bel with the planet Jupiter, which, with the planet Venus (under the name Astarte or Astaroth), was worshipped in the East as the god of fortune, the most propitious star to be born under (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.65.11">Is 65:11</reference>). According to the Apocryphal book, Bel and the Dragon, Bel was cast down by Cyrus.<div eID="gen15710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">boweth ... stoopeth--</hi>falleth prostrate (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.4">Is 10:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.5.3">1Sa 5:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.5.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.20.8">Psa 20:8</reference>).<div eID="gen15711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15712" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Nebo--</hi>the planet Mercury or Hermes, in astrology. The scribe of heaven, answering to the Egyptian Anubis. The extensive worship of it is shown by the many proper names compounded of it: Nebuchadnezzar. Nebuzar-adan, Nabonassar, &c.<div eID="gen15712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15713" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">were upon--</hi>that is, were a burden (supplied from the following clause) upon. It was customary to transport the gods of the vanquished to the land of the conquerors, who thought thereby the more effectually to keep down the subject people (<reference osisRef="1Sam.5.1">1Sa 5:1</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.7">Jr 48:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.3">49:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.8">Da 11:8</reference>).<div eID="gen15713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15714" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">carriages--</hi>in the Old English sense of the things carried, the images borne by you: the lading (<reference osisRef="Acts.21.15">Ac 21:15</reference>), "carriages," not the vehicles, but the baggage. Or, the images which used to be carried by you formerly in your solemn processions [Maurer].<div eID="gen15714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15715" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">were heavy loaden--</hi>rather, are put as a load on the beasts of burden [Maurer]. Horsley translates, "They who should have been your carriers (as Jehovah is to His people, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.3">Is 46:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.4">4</reference>) are become burdens" (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.46.4">Is 46:4</reference>). <div eID="gen15715" type="x-p"/>
entries.158b7f09c3bd560c612a73cd62c6bd53018e6a89: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9214"/><div sID="gen15716" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9214"/><hi type="bold">2. deliver--</hi>from the enemies' hands.<div eID="gen15716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15717" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burden--</hi>their images laid on the beasts (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.1">Is 46:1</reference>).<div eID="gen15717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">themselves--</hi>the gods, here also distinguished from their images. <div eID="gen15718" type="x-p"/>
entries.424fca1f751a8834cebae93334b121b5ccb4897b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9215"/><div sID="gen15719" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9215"/>3. in contrast to what precedes: Babylon's idols, so far from bearing its people safely are themselves borne off, a burden to the laden beast; but Jehovah bears His people in safety even from the womb to old age (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Is 63:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">De 32:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.71.6">Psa 71:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.18">18</reference>). God compares Himself to a nurse tenderly carrying a child; contrast Moses' language (<reference osisRef="Num.11.12">Nu 11:12</reference>). <div eID="gen15719" type="x-p"/>
entries.b01bcfe08a24ed12931066c7534646622714cd5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9216"/><div sID="gen15720" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9216"/><hi type="bold">4. old age--</hi>As "your"--"you"--"you," are not in the Hebrew, the sentiment is more general than English Version, though of course it includes the Jews from the infancy to the more advanced age of their history (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.6">Is 47:6</reference>).<div eID="gen15720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15721" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am he--</hi>that is, the same (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.27">Psa 102:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.24">Joh 8:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.8">He 13:8</reference>).<div eID="gen15721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15722" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will bear ... carry--</hi>Not only do I not need to be borne and carried Myself, as the idols (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.1">Is 46:1</reference>). <div eID="gen15722" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0d0f05e8c1ef7163eff2683f33cc03838dd853e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9217"/><div sID="gen15723" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9217"/>5. (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.18">Is 40:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.25">25</reference>). <div eID="gen15723" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c218b39e7854ced2a8e039d710cc9097f0e6738: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9218"/><div sID="gen15724" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9218"/>6. (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.19">Is 40:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.7">41:7</reference>.) They lavish gold out of their purses and spare no expense for their idol. Their profuseness shames the niggardliness of professors who worship God with what cost them nothing. Sin is always a costly service. <div eID="gen15724" type="x-p"/>
entries.4394970c8846b0a800c4f82c4e71d227834e11d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9219"/><div sID="gen15725" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9219"/><hi type="bold">7. cry ... can ... not ... save--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.45.20">Is 45:20</reference>, with which contrast <reference osisRef="Isa.45.19">Is 45:19</reference>). <div eID="gen15725" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e0e8ddca1e647278de755572f6330fdc9b54c88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9220"/><div sID="gen15726" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9220"/><hi type="bold">8. show yourselves men--</hi>Renounce the childishness of idolatry as shown in what precedes (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.20">1Co 14:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.13">16:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.14">Ep 4:14</reference>). In order to be manly we must be godly; for man was made "in the image of God," and only rises to his true dignity when joined to God; virtue is derived from the Latin vir, "a man."<div eID="gen15726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring ... to mind--</hi>rather, "lay it to heart."<div eID="gen15727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">transgressors--</hi>addressed to the idolaters among the Jews. <div eID="gen15728" type="x-p"/>
entries.9802e77c5cd6204de3931ef6317b5411e8f68f70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9221"/><div sID="gen15729" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9221"/><hi type="bold">9. former--</hi>namely, proofs of the sole Godship of Jehovah, from predictions fulfilled, and interpositions of God in behalf of Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.5">Is 45:5</reference>). <div eID="gen15729" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ce3c4f8f97d5141c56d975b3408392a57af6e7f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9222"/><div sID="gen15730" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9222"/>10. (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.21">Is 45:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.22">41:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">44:26</reference>).<div eID="gen15730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet--</hi>not in the Hebrew. Translate, "What had not been done" [Horsley].<div eID="gen15731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15732" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">do all my pleasure--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Is 53:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.19">Ro 9:19</reference>). <div eID="gen15732" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a6fa07ab669c0d365ac8bd27cfbe2dc10a684e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9223"/><div sID="gen15733" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9223"/><hi type="bold">11. ravenous bird--</hi>Cyrus so called on account of the rapidity of his marches from the distant regions of Persia to pounce on his prey (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.41.2">Is 41:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.25">Is 41:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">Jr 49:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference>). The standard of Cyrus, too, was a golden eagle on a spear (see the heathen historian, Xenophon, 7, where almost the same word is used, aetos, as here, ayit).<div eID="gen15733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15734" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">executeth my counsel--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Is 44:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.13">45:13</reference>). Babylon represents, mystically, the apostate faction: the destruction of its idols symbolizes the future general extirpation of all idolatry and unbelief.<div eID="gen15734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">purposed ... also do it--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.43.13">Is 43:13</reference>). <div eID="gen15735" type="x-p"/>
entries.083c8d24c96f22cdbe5ce41d5b9e7efc949de01c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9224"/><div sID="gen15736" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9224"/><hi type="bold">12. stout-hearted--</hi>stubborn in resisting God (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.5">Psa 76:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.51">Ac 7:51</reference>).<div eID="gen15736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15737" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">far from righteousness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.59.9">Is 59:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">Ha 2:4</reference>). <div eID="gen15737" type="x-p"/>
entries.6fc414e988e154800f75a7b7a15097abd19dc762: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9225"/><div sID="gen15738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9225"/><hi type="bold">13. near--</hi>antithetical to "far" (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.12">Is 46:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.5">Is 51:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.56.1">56:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">61:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.6-Rom.10.8">Ro 10:6-8</reference>).<div eID="gen15738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>answering to "salvation" in the parallel clause; therefore it means here, "my righteous deliverance"; righteous, because proving the truth of God's promises, and so contrived as to not compromise, but vindicate, His righteousness (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.21">Is 42:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.26">Ro 3:26</reference>).<div eID="gen15739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zion ... my glory--</hi>rather, "I will give salvation in Zion; to Israel (I will give) my glory" [Horsley]. (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.11">Is 63:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.14.7">Psa 14:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.32">Lu 2:32</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.46"/>

entries.a7c167e1a1f4905237dfa1282c99b1433c77d909: <div eID="gen28367" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28368" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28369" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28369" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28368" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28370" type="x-p"/> The idols of Babylon represented as so far from being able to bear the burden of their votaries, that they themselves are borne by beasts of burden into captivity, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.1">Isa 46:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.2">Isa 46:2</reference>. This beautifully contrasted with the tender care of God, in bearing his people from first to last in his arms, and delivering them from their distress, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.3">Isa 46:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.4">Isa 46:4</reference>. The prophet, then, with his usual force and elegance, goes on to show the folly of idolatry, and the utter inability of idols, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.5-Isa.46.7">Isa 46:5-7</reference>. From which he passes with great ease to the contemplation of the attributes and perfections of the true God, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.8-Isa.46.10">Isa 46:8-10</reference>. Particularly that prescience which foretold the deliverance of the Jews from the Babylonish captivity, with all its leading circumstances; and also that very remote event of which it is the type in the days of the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.11-Isa.46.13">Isa 46:11-13</reference>. <div eID="gen28370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28371" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen28371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28372" type="x-p"/> Their carriages were heavy loaden "Their burdens are heavy" - For נשאתיכם nesuotheychem, your burdens, the Septuagint had in their copy נשאתיהם nesuotheyhem, their burdens.
entries.2d82c679113c089bfab3a5b02e1c95cfb189314c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen28372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28373" type="x-p"/> They could not deliver the burden "They could not deliver their own charge" - That is, their worshippers, who ought to have been borne by them. See the two next verses. The Chaldee and Syriac Versions render it in effect to the same purpose, those that bear them, meaning their worshippers; but how they can render משא massa in an active sense, I do not understand. <div eID="gen28373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28374" type="x-p"/> For לא lo, not, ולא velo, and they could not, is the reading of twenty-four of Kennicott's, sixteen of De Rossi's, and two of my own MSS. The added ו vau gives more elegance to the passage. <div eID="gen28374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28375" type="x-p"/> But themselves "Even they themselves" - For ונפשם venaphsham, an ancient MS. has כי נפשם ki naphsham, with more force.
entries.afc42ccfd2ec37123c8c34cdbd477471a8ab9a0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen28375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28376" type="x-p"/> Which are borne by me from the belly "Ye that have been borne by me from the birth" - The prophet very ingeniously, and with great force, contrasts the power of God, and his tender goodness effectually exerted towards his people, with the inability of the false gods of the heathen. He like an indulgent father had carried his people in his arms, "as a man carrieth his son," <reference osisRef="Deu.1.31">Deu 1:31</reference>. He had protected them, and delivered them from their distresses: whereas the idols of the heathen are forced to be carried about themselves and removed from place to place, with great labor and fatigue, by their worshippers; nor can they answer, or deliver their votaries, when they cry unto them. <div eID="gen28376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28377" type="x-p"/> Moses, expostulating with God on the weight of the charge laid upon him as leader of his people, expresses that charge under the same image of a parent's carrying his children, in very strong terms: "Have I conceived all this people? have I begotten them? that thou shouldest say unto me, Carry them in thy bosom, as a nursing father beareth the sucking child, unto the land which thou swarest unto their fathers;" <reference osisRef="Num.11.12">Num 11:12</reference>.
entries.96b594769d7bc6e742026fd96799469b838efdaa: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen28377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28378" type="x-p"/> They bear him upon the shoulder - and set him in his place - This is the way in which the Hindoos carry their gods; and indeed so exact a picture is this of the idolatrous procession of this people, that the prophet might almost be supposed to have been sitting among the Hindoos when he delivered this prophecy. - Ward'S Customs. <div eID="gen28378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28379" type="x-p"/> Pindar has treated with a just and very elegant ridicule the work of the statuary even in comparison with his own poetry, from this circumstance of its being fixed to a certain station. "The friends of Pytheas," says the Scholiast, "came to the poet, desiring him to write an ode on his victory. Pindar demanded three drachms, (minae, I suppose it should be), for the ode. No, say they, we can have a brazen statue for that money, which will be better than a poem. However, changing their minds afterwards, they came and offered him what he had demanded." This gave him the hint of the following ingenious esordium of his ode: - Ουκ ανδριαντοποιος ειμ' Ὡστ' ελινυσσοντα μ' εργαζε- σθαι αγαλματ' επ' αυτας βαθμιδος Ἑσταοτ.Αλλ' επι πασας Ὁλκαδος εν τ' ακατῳ γλυκει' αοιδα Στειχ' απ' Αιγινας διαγγελ- lois' ὁτι Λαμπωνος ὑιος Πυθεας ευρυσθενης Νικῃ Νεμειοις παγκρατιου στεφανον. <div eID="gen28379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28380" type="x-p"/> Nem. v. <div eID="gen28380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28381" type="x-p"/> Thus elegantly translated by Mr. Francis in a note to Hor. Carm. 4:2. 19. "It is not mine with forming hand <div eID="gen28381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28382" type="x-p"/> To bid a lifeless image stand <div eID="gen28382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28383" type="x-p"/> For ever on its base: <div eID="gen28383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28384" type="x-p"/> But fly, my verses, and proclaim <div eID="gen28384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28385" type="x-p"/> To distant realms, with deathless fame, <div eID="gen28385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28386" type="x-p"/> That Pytheas conquered in the rapid race." <div eID="gen28386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28387" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.3-Jer.10.5">Jer 10:3-5</reference>, seems to be indebted to Isaiah for most of the following passage: - "The practices of the people are altogether vanity: <div eID="gen28387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28388" type="x-p"/> For they cut down a tree from the forest; <div eID="gen28388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28389" type="x-p"/> The work of the artificer's hand with the axe; <div eID="gen28389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28390" type="x-p"/> With silver and with gold it is adorned; <div eID="gen28390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28391" type="x-p"/> With nails and with hammers it is fastened, that it may not totter. <div eID="gen28391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28392" type="x-p"/> Like the palm-tree they stand stiff, and cannot speak; <div eID="gen28392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28393" type="x-p"/> They are carried about, for they cannot go: <div eID="gen28393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28394" type="x-p"/> Fear them not, for they cannot do harm; <div eID="gen28394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28395" type="x-p"/> Neither is it in them to do good."
entries.39213e8d0e3dfd7dc276c4e26c4db45192b154df: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen28395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28396" type="x-p"/> Show yourselves men - התאששו hithoshashu. This word is rather of doubtful derivation and signification. It occurs only in this place: and some of the ancient interpreters seem to have had something different in their copies. The Vulgate read התבששו hithbosheshu, take shame to yourselves; the Syriac התבוננו hithbonenu, consider with yourselves; the Septuagint στεναξετε· perhaps התאבלו hithabbelu, groan or mourn, within yourselves. Several MSS. read התאוששו hithosheshu, but without any help to the sense.
entries.455e1f38eb74235d6dd789b8565388d951e6d222: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen28396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28397" type="x-p"/> Calling a ravenous bird from the east "Calling from the east the eagle" - A very proper emblem for Cyrus, as in other respects, so particularly because the ensign of Cyrus was a golden eagle, ΑΕΤΟΣ χρυσους, the very word עיט ayit, which the prophet uses here, expressed as near as may be in Greek letters. Xenoph. Cyrop. lib. 7 sub. init. Kimchi says his father understood this, not of Cyrus, but of the Messiah. <div eID="gen28397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28398" type="x-p"/> From a far country "From a land far distant" - Two MSS. add the conjunction ו vau, ומארץ umeerets; and so the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate.
entries.217b96c33112ba9c4ef46089b3ea3c23a0bec26c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen28398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28399" type="x-p"/> Hearken unto me, ye stout-hearted - This is an address to the Babylonians, stubbornly bent on the practice of injustice towards the Israelites.  <chapter eID="Isa.46"/> <div eID="gen28399" type="x-p"/>

entries.059b6fca5803f7d598d96c112dc3a34a78a1e1a1: <reference osisRef="Isa.46.1-Isa.46.2">Isa 46:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen13435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13436" type="x-p"/> There follows now a trilogy of prophecies referring to Babylon. After the prophet has shown what Israel has to expect of Cyrus, he turns to what awaits Babylon at the hands of Cyrus. <hi type="italic">“Bel sinketh down, Nebo stoopeth; its images come to the beast of burden and draught cattle: your litters are laden, a burden for the panting. They stopped, sank down all at once, and could not get rid of the burden; and their own self went into captivity.”</hi> The reference to Babylon comes out at once in the names of the gods. <hi type="italic">Bēl</hi> was the Jupiter of the Babylonians and, as <hi type="italic">Bel-Merodach</hi>, the tutelar deity of Babylon; <hi type="italic">Nebo</hi> was Mercury, the tutelar deity of the later Chaldean royal family, as the many kings’ names in which it appears clearly show (e.g., <hi type="italic">Mabonassar</hi>, <hi type="italic">Nabo-polassar</hi>, etc.). The pryamidal heap of ruins on the right bank of the Euphrates, which is now called <hi type="italic">Birs Nimrud</hi>, is the ruin of the temple of Bel, of which Herodotus gives a description in i. 181-183, and probably also of the tower mentioned in Gen 11, which was dedicated to Bel, if not to <hi type="italic">El</hi> = Saturn. Herodotus describes two golden statues of Bel which were found there (cf., Diodorus, ii. 9, 5), but the way in which Nebo was represented is still unknown. The judgment of Jehovah falls upon these gods through Cyrus. Bel suddenly falls headlong, and Nebo stoops till he also falls. Their images come to (fall to the lot of) the <hi type="italic">chayyâh</hi>, i.e., the camels, dromedaries, and elephants; and <hi type="italic">behēmâh</hi>, i.e., horses, oxen, and asses. Your נשׂאת, <hi type="italic">gestamina</hi>, the prophet exclaims to the Babylonians, i.e., the images hitherto carried by you in solemn procession (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.20">Isa 45:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.26">Amo 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.5">Jer 10:5</reference>), are now packed up, a burden for that which is wearied out, i.e., for cattle that has become weary with carrying them. In <reference osisRef="Isa.46.1">Isa 46:1</reference>, as the two participial clauses show, the prophet still takes his stand in the midst of the catastrophe; but in <reference osisRef="Isa.46.2">Isa 46:2</reference> it undoubtedly lies behind him as a completed act. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.46.2">Isa 46:2</reference></hi> he continues, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.46.1">Isa 46:1</reference>, to enter into the delusion of the heathen, and distinguish between the <hi type="italic">numina</hi> and <hi type="italic">simulacra</hi>. The gods of Babylon have all stooped at once, have sunken down, and have been unable to save their images which were packed upon the cattle, out of the hands of the conquerors. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.46.2">Isa 46:2</reference></hi> he destroys this delusion: they are going into captivity (Hos 10:5; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.7">Jer 48:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.3">Jer 49:3</reference>), even “their ownself” (<hi type="italic">naphshâm</hi>), since the self or personality of the beingless beings consists of nothing more than the wood and metal of which their images are composed.
entries.aa206c3b5640572accb1e5e0a0396e2afc68fda3: <reference osisRef="Isa.46.3-Isa.46.5">Isa 46:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen13436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13437" type="x-p"/> From this approaching reduction of the gods of Babylon to their original nothingness, several admonitions are now derived. The first admonition is addressed to all Israel. <hi type="italic">“Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel: ye, lifted up from the womb; ye, carried from the mother’s lap! And till old age it is I, and to grey hair I shall bear you on my shoulder: I have done it, and I shall carry; and I put upon my shoulder, and deliver. To whom can ye compare me, and liken, and place side by side, that we should be equal?”</hi> The house of Jacob is Judah here, as in Oba 1:18 (see Caspari on the passage), <reference osisRef="Nah.2.3">Nah 2:3</reference>, and the house of Israel the same as the house of Joseph in Obadiah; whereas in <reference osisRef="Amos.3.13">Amo 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Amo 6:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.7.2">Amo 7:2</reference>, Jacob stands for Israel, in distinction from Judah. The Assyrian exile was earlier than the Babylonian, and had already naturalized the greater part of the exiles in a heathen land, and robbed them of their natural character, so that there was only a remnant left by whom there was any hope that the prophet’s message would be received. What the exiles of both houses were to hear was the question in <reference osisRef="Isa.46.5">Isa 46:5</reference>, which called upon them to consider the incomparable nature of their God, as deduced from what Jehovah could say of Himself in relation to all Israel, and what He does say from העמסים onwards. Babylon carried its idols, but all in vain: they were carried forth, without being able to save themselves; but Jehovah carried His people, and saved them. The expressions, “from the womb, and from the mother’s lap,” point back to the time when the nation which had been in process of formation from the time of Abraham onwards came out of Egypt, and was born, as it were, into the light of the world. From this time forward it had lain upon Jehovah like a willingly adopted burden, and He had carried it as a nurse carries a suckling (Num 11:12), and an eagle its young (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">Deu 32:11</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Isa.46.4">Isa 46:4</reference> the attributes of the people are carried on in direct (not relative) self-assertions on the part of Jehovah. The <hi type="italic">senectus</hi> and <hi type="italic">canities</hi> are obviously those of the people - not, however, as though it was already in a state of dotage (as Hitzig maintains, appealing erroneously to <reference osisRef="Isa.47.6">Isa 47:6</reference>), but as denoting the future and latest periods of its history. Even till then Jehovah is He, i.e., the Absolute, and always the same (see <reference osisRef="Isa.41.4">Isa 41:4</reference>). As He has acted in the past, so will He act at all times - supporting and saving His people. Hence He could properly ask, Whom could you place by the side of me, so that we should be equal? (<hi type="italic">Vav consec.</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.25">Isa 40:25</reference>).
entries.f7cfb8411e83af9439ccc3c18e73d995a517d7ad: <reference osisRef="Isa.46.6-Isa.46.7">Isa 46:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen13437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13438" type="x-p"/> The negative answer to this question is the direct result of what precedes, but a still further proof is given in <reference osisRef="Isa.46.6">Isa 46:6</reference>, Isa 46:7. <hi type="italic">“They who pour gold out of the bag, and weigh silver with the balance, hire a goldsmith to make it into a god, that they may fall down, yea, throw themselves down. They lift it up, carry it away upon their shoulder, and set it down in its place: there it stands; from its place it does not move: men also cry to it, but it does not answer; it saves no one out of distress.”</hi> There is no necessity for assuming that הזּלים is used in the place of the finite verb, as Hitzig imagines, or as equivalent to זלים הם, as Rosenmüller and Gesenius suppose; but up to ישׂכּרוּ the whole is subject, and therefore ישׁקלוּ is the point at which the change into the finite verb occurs (Ges. §131, 2). The point in <hi type="italic">hazzâlı̄m</hi> is not the extravagant expenditure, as Ewald thinks, but the mean origin of the god, which commences with the pouring out of gold from a purse (<hi type="italic">zūl</hi> = <hi type="italic">zâlal</hi>, to shake, to pour out). <hi type="italic">Qâneh</hi> is the lever of the scales (κανών). The metal weighed out is given to a goldsmith, who plates the idol with the gold, and makes the ornaments for it of silver. When it is finished, they lift it up, or shoulder it (ישּׂאהוּ with a distinctive Great Telisha), carry it home, and set it down in the place which it is to have <hi type="italic">under it</hi> (תּחתּיו). There it stands firm, immoveable, and also deaf and dumb, hearing no one, answering no one, and helping no one. The subject to יצעק is any צעק. The first admonition closes here. The gods who are carried fall without being able to save themselves, whereas Israel’s God carries and saves His people; He, the Incomparable, more especially in contrast with the lifeless puppets of idols.
entries.07fbb03df9341963124f59de4eea6b7e681d89da: <reference osisRef="Isa.46.8-Isa.46.11">Isa 46:8-11</reference> <div eID="gen13438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13439" type="x-p"/> The second admonition is addressed to those who would imitate the heathen. <hi type="italic">“Remember this, and become firm, take it to heart, ye rebellious ones! Remember the beginning from the olden time, that I am God, and none else: Deity, and absolutely none like me: proclaiming the issue from the beginning, and from ancient times what has not yet taken place, saying, My counsel shall stand, and all my good pleasure I carry out: calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a distant land: not only have I spoken, I also bring it; I have purposed it, I also execute it.”</hi> The object to which “this” points back is the nothingness of idols and idolatry. The persons addressed are the פושׁעים (those apostatizing), but, as התאשׁשׁוּ shows, whether it mean ἀνδιρίζεσθε or κραταιοῦσθε (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.13">1Co 16:13</reference>), such as have not yet actually carried out their rebellion or apostasy, but waver between Jehovahism and heathenism, and are inclined to the latter. התאשׁשׁו is hardly a denom. <hi type="italic">hithpalel</hi> of אישׁ in the sense of “man yourselves,” since אישׁ, whether it signifies a husband or a social being, or like אנושׁ, a frail or mortal being, is at any rate equivalent to אנשׁ, and therefore never shows the modification u. אשׁשׁ (אשׁה) signifies to be firm, strong, compact; in the <hi type="italic">piel</hi> (rabb.), to be well-grounded; <hi type="italic">nithpael</hi>, to be fortified, established; here <hi type="italic">hithpoel</hi>, “show yourselves firm” (Targ., Jer.: <hi type="italic">fundamini ne rursum subitus idololatriae vos turbo subvertat</hi>). That they may strengthen themselves in faith and fidelity, they are referred to the history of their nation; ראשׁנות are not prophecies given at an earlier time - a meaning which the <hi type="italic">priora</hi> only acquire in such a connection as <reference osisRef="Isa.43.9">Isa 43:9</reference> - but former occurrences. They are to pass before their minds the earlier history, and indeed “from the olden time.” “<hi type="italic">Remember:</hi>” <hi type="italic">zikhrū</hi> is connected with the accusative of the object of remembrance, and כּי points to its result. An earnest and thoughtful study of history would show them that Jehovah alone was <hi type="italic">El</hi>, the absolutely Mighty One, and <hi type="italic">'Elōhı̄m</hi>, the Being who united in Himself all divine majesty by which reverence was evoked. The participles in <reference osisRef="Isa.46.10">Isa 46:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.11">Isa 46:11</reference> are attached to the “I” of כּמוני. It is Jehovah, the Incomparable, who has now, as at other times from the very commencement of the new turn in history, predicted the issue of which it would lead, and <hi type="italic">miqqedem</hi>, i.e., long before, predicted things that have not yet occurred, and which therefore lit outside the sphere of human combination - another passage like <reference osisRef="Isa.41.26">Isa 41:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.21">Isa 45:21</reference>, etc., in which what is predicted in these prophecies lays claim to the character of a prediction of long standing, and not of one merely uttered a few years before. The ראשׁית, in which the ראשׁנות are already in progress (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.9">Isa 42:9</reference>), is to be regarded as the prophet’s ideal present; for Jehovah not only foretells before the appearance of Cyrus what is to be expected of him, but declares that His determination must be realized, that He will bring to pass everything upon which His will is set, and summons the man upon the stage of history as the instrument of its accomplishment, so that He knew Cyrus before he himself had either consciousness or being (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.4-Isa.45.5">Isa 45:4-5</reference>). The east is Persis (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.2">Isa 41:2</reference>); and the distant land, the northern part of Media (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.5">Isa 13:5</reference>). Cyrus is called an eagle, or, strictly speaking, a bird of prey (<hi type="italic">‛ayit</hi>),<note placement="foot">The resemblance to ἀετός (αἰετός) is merely accidental. This name for the eagle is traceable, like <hi type="italic">avid</hi>, to a root <hi type="italic">vâ</hi>, to move with the swiftness of the wind. This was shown by Passow, compare Kuhn’s <hi type="italic">Zeitschrift</hi>, i. 29, where we also find at 10, 126 another but less probable derivation from a root <hi type="italic">i</hi>, to go (compare <hi type="italic">eva</hi>, a course).</note> just as in <reference osisRef="Jer.49.22">Jer 49:22</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference> Nebuchadnezzar is called a <hi type="italic">nesher</hi>. According to <hi type="italic">Cyrop.</hi> vii. 1, 4, the campaign of Cyrus was ἀετὸς χρυσοῦς ἐπὶ δόρατος μακροῦ ἀνατεταμένος. Instead of עצתו אישׁ, the <hi type="italic">keri</hi> reads more clearly, though quite unnecessarily, (עצתי אישׁ (see e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">Isa 44:26</reference>). The correlate אף (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.46.11">Isa 46:11</reference></hi>), which is only attached to the second verb the second time, affirms that Jehovah does not only the one, but the other also. His word is made by Him into a deed, His idea into a reality. יצר is a word used particularly by Isaiah, to denote the ideal preformation of the future in the mind of God (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.26">Isa 37:26</reference>). The feminine suffixes refer in a neuter sense to the theme of the prophecy - the overthrow of idolatrous Babel, upon which Cyrus comes down like an eagle, in the strength of Jehovah. So far we have the <hi type="italic">nota bene</hi> for those who are inclined to apostasy. They are to lay to heart the nothingness of the heathen gods, and, on the other hand, the self-manifestation of Jehovah from the olden time, that is to say, of the One God who is now foretelling and carrying out the destruction of the imperial city through the eagle from the east.
entries.753f575fd72c0bf205ac9ac677dfed7e3427858c: <reference osisRef="Isa.46.12-Isa.46.13">Isa 46:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen13439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13440" type="x-p"/> A third admonition is addressed to the forts esprits in <reference osisRef="Isa.46.12">Isa 46:12</reference>, Isa 46:13. <hi type="italic">“Hearken to me, ye strong-hearted, that are far from righteousness! I have brought my righteousness near; it is not far off, and my salvation tarrieth not: and I give salvation in Zion, my glory to Israel.”</hi> All that is called in Hellenic and Hellenistic νοῦς λόγος συνείδησις θυμός, is comprehended in καρδία; and everything by which <hi type="italic">bâsâr</hi> and <hi type="italic">nephesh</hi> are affected comes into the light of consciousness in the heart (<hi type="italic">Psychol.</hi> p. 251). According to this biblico-psychological idea, לב אבּיתי may signify either the courageous (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.6">Psa 76:6</reference>), or, as in this instance, the strong-minded; but as a synonym of לב סהזקי (<reference osisRef="Ezek.2.4">Eze 2:4</reference>) and לב קשׁי (<reference osisRef="Ezek.3.7">Eze 3:7</reference>), viz., in the sense of those who resist the impressions of the work and grace of God in their consciousness of mental superiority to anything of the kind, and not in the sense of those who have great mental endowments. These are “far from righteousness” (<hi type="italic">tsedâqâh</hi>), that is to say, they have despaired of the true, loving fidelity of Jehovah, and have no wish for any further knowledge of it. Therefore they shall hear, and possibly not without impression, that this loving fidelity is about to manifest itself, and salvation is about to be realized. Jehovah has given salvation in Zion, that is to say, is giving it even now, so that it will become once more the centre of the renovated nation, and impart its glory to this, so that it may shine in the splendour bestowed upon it by its God. We have here the side of light and love, turned towards us by the two-faced <hi type="italic">tsedâqâh</hi>, as a parallel word to <hi type="italic">theshū‛âh</hi>, or salvation. With this admonition to the indifferent and careless, to whom the salvation of which they have given up all hope is proclaimed as at the door, this prophecy is brought to a close. In three distinct stages, commencing with “hearken,” “remember,” “hearken,” it has unfolded the spiritual influences which the fact declared in <reference osisRef="Isa.46.1">Isa 46:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.2">Isa 46:2</reference> ought to have upon Israel, and resembles a pastoral sermon in its tone.  <chapter eID="Isa.46"/> <div eID="gen13440" type="x-p"/>

entries.d1613d86277ac2efd9c2e56615d023de4b5ceee0: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.46.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.46.1" sID="gen49158" type="section"/> <div sID="gen49159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi><hi type="italic"> Bel hath bowed down. </hi>Isaiah continues the same subject; for we need not trouble ourselves about the division of chapters, which have not always been accurately divided; but we ought to examine the statements themselves, which agree with each other in the manner which I have pointed out. Yet if any prefer to view this as the commencement of a new discourse, because immediately afterwards he prophesies concerning the destruction of Babylon, I shall not greatly quarrel with him.<div eID="gen49159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49160" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Nebo is cast down. </hi>“Bel” and “Nebo” were idols which were worshipped by the Babylonians, and probably were their chief patrons; as idolaters always have some particular gods, under whose protection, above all others, they consider themselves to be placed. It may be conjectured that this “Nebo” was a sort of inferior god that was added to the chief god “Bel,” as Mercury was to Jupiter. Under their names he includes also the rest of the idols, and declares that all the superstitions and false worship of the Gentiles shall be overthrown, when God shall lay low and triumph over their worshippers; because it shall then be manifest that he is the righteous avenger of his Church.<div eID="gen49160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49161" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Their idols shall be on the beasts. </hi>The Babylonians having haughtily boasted of the protection of false gods, the Prophet rebukes that vain confidence, because the God of Israel will not only bring utter ruin on that wicked nation, but also will cast down and treat disdainfully their gods. The reason why he says that they shall be burdens of <hi type="italic">“beasts” </hi>is, that they shall be laid on waggons and removed from one place to another, and shall even be huddled together without any respect, as the waggoners think proper. This is what is meant by “being cast down,” for the robbers shall collect into a large heap those gods which formerly occupied an elevated station.<div eID="gen49161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49162" type="x-p"/>There can be no doubt, indeed, that this was fulfilled when the Persians and Medes took Babylon by storm; for when the monarchy was removed, these idols were taken away as a part of the booty. But Isaiah, though he predicted this, looked farther, that is, to the coming of Christ, who was to overtum and destroy all false worship; for, when his kingdom has been established, all idols immediately fall to the ground, and it is impossible that false religion and superstition can exist along with the knowledge of him. By his brightness he dispels all darkness, so as to leave no room for false gods or superstitions; for, as Paul says,<div eID="gen49162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49163" type="x-p"/>“What hath Christ to do with Belial? What hath light to do with darkness?” <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.6.14 Bible:2Cor.6.15">2 Corinthians 6:14,15</reference>.)<div eID="gen49163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49164" type="x-p"/>At the same time it ought to be observed, that the Prophet had his eye on the time when the Jews were held in captivity; for they saw the Babylonians offer incense to idols, and ascribe to them supreme power, as if the government of affairs depended on them; while the God of the Jews was treated with scorn, as if he could not defend his people, or as if he cared nothing about them. For this reason he shews that there will be so great a revolution, that the gods of the Babylonians, which were elevated so high, shall be laid low, and God, who appeared to he low, shall rise up and avenge his people.<div eID="gen49164" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.46.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen49158" osisID="Isa.46.1" type="section"/>
entries.23d74b33d19a7d044c5c193eba7f42126c138c21: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.46.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.46.2" sID="gen49165" type="section"/> <div sID="gen49166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi><hi type="italic"> They could not withdraw themselves from the burden. </hi>He ridicules the vanity of such gods as these, which have neither strength nor motion, and cannot defend or support themselves, and, in a word, who need the aid of beasts of burden to carry them. There is, therefore, an implied contrast between idols and the true God, who has no need of anything whatever. I interpret these words as applied to beasts, but the Prophet heightens the disgrace by saying that they were a heavy burden to the beasts themselves which would willingly have cast them off, and consequently that the false gods, besides being of no use to their worshippers, also wearied out the beasts.<div eID="gen49166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49167" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And their soul hath gone into captivity. </hi>This is a Hebrew mode of expression, by which he ridicules those gods which have neither “soul” nor understanding. He speaks ironically, therefore, against useless and dumb idols, when he says that they shall be carried into captivity along with their soul. But we must see if these things cannot be retorted on the true God, whose ark, by which he gave testimony of his presence, was taken by the Philistines; for in this way it appeared as if the Lord were a captive. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Sam.4.11">1 Samuel 4:11</reference>.) This objection may be easily answered; for, although the Lord intended that the ark should be a testimony of his presence, yet he forbade the Jews to fix their whole and exclusive attention upon it, but commanded them to raise their eyes to heaven, and there to seek and adore God. He wished to be always worshipped in a spiritual manner, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.4.24">John 4:24</reference>,) and the ark was not adored instead of God, but was a symbol, by which the people were led upwards, as by the hand, to God. The Gentiles, on the other hand, fixed their attention on their idols, and attributed to them divine power.<div eID="gen49167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49168" type="x-p"/>It might even have been said that the Philistines were at length punished for their wickedness, and acknowledged that they had to deal with the true God. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Sam.5.6">1 Samuel 5:6</reference>.) But that would not have been a sufficient answer, because the Lord sometimes permitted his ark to be treated with derision, as is evident from other passages of the history. The true solution therefore is, that the Lord, though he holds intercourse with us by symbols and sacraments, yet wishes to be sought in heaven. To this must be added, that he had openly declared, by memorable predictions, that he was not dragged as a captive by conquerors, but that of his own accord he exposed his sanctuary to the sport of enemies, in order to punish the sins of his people. Nor could the Jews, when the Temple had been thrown down and bumt, and when the holy vessels were carried to Babylon, doubt that the same God whom they had worshipped was the author of this punishment, since he had so frequently threatened by his prophets what then happened.<div eID="gen49168" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.46.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen49165" osisID="Isa.46.2" type="section"/>
entries.eb6452d9ecaef03af527eb01fbd4e0a13dfa862b: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.46.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.46.3" sID="gen49169" type="section"/> <div sID="gen49170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi><hi type="italic"> Hear me. </hi>Here the Prophet beautifully points out the vast difference between the true God and idols. Having formerly said that the Babylonian gods must be drawn on waggons and carts, because they consist of dead matter, he now ascribes a widely different office to the God of Israel, namely, that he “carries” his people, like a mother, who carries the child in her womb, and afterwards carries it in her bosom. He addresses the Jews, that they may return an answer from their experience; for this ought to have powerfully affected them, when they actually felt that he bore them and their burdens. He, therefore, makes use of a highly appropriate contrast, and concludes from the preceding statements: “Acknowledge that I am the true God, and that I differ widely from idols, which are useless and dead weights; for you have known and experienced my power by constant benefits, which I have not ceased to confer upon you from the womb.” God is not only powerful in himself, but diffuses his power through all the creatures; so that we feel his strength and energy.<div eID="gen49170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49171" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Who are carried from the womb. </hi>This is a very expressive metaphor, by which God compares himself to a mother who carries a child in her womb. He speaks of the past time, when he began to give them testimonies of his grace. Yet the words might be taken as meaning simply that God kindly nourished that people, like an infant taken from its mother’s womb, and carried it in his bosom, as the Psalmist says,<div eID="gen49171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49172" type="x-p"/>“I was cast upon thee from the womb, thou art my God from my mother’s belly.” <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.22.10">Psalm 22:10</reference>.)<div eID="gen49172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49173" type="x-p"/>But as God did not only begin to act as the father and nurse of his people from the time when they were born, but also “begat them” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jas.1.18">James 1:18</reference>) spiritually, I do not object to extending the words so far as to mean, that they were brought, as it were, out of the bowels of God into a new life and the hope of an eternal inheritance.<div eID="gen49173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49174" type="x-p"/>If it be objected, that God is everywhere called “a Father,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.31.9">Jeremiah 31:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Mal.1.6">Malachi 1:6</reference>,) and that this title is more appropriate to him, I reply, that no figures of speech can describe God’s extraordinary affection towards us; for it is infinite and various; so that, if all that can be said or imagined about love were brought together into one, yet it would be surpassed by the greatness of the love of God. By no metaphor, therefore, can his incomparable goodness be described. If you understand it, simply to mean that God, from the time that he begat them, gently carried and nourished them in his bosom, this will agree admirably with what we find in the Song of Moses,<div eID="gen49174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49175" type="x-p"/>“He bore them, and carried them, as an eagle carrieth her young on her wings.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.11">Deuteronomy 32:11</reference>.)<div eID="gen49175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49176" type="x-p"/>In a word, the intention of the Prophet is to shew, that the Jews, if they do not choose to forget their descent, cannot arrive at any other conclusion than that they were not begotten in vain, and that God, who has manifested himself to be both their Father and their Mother, will always assist them; and likewise, that they have known his power by uninterrupted experience, so that they ought not to pay homage to idols.<div eID="gen49176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen49177" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">All the remnant of the house of Israel. </hi>By calling them a “remnant” he means, as we formerly remarked, that the greater part had been alienated from the Church by their revolt, so that the hope of deliverance belonged only to a very small number. On this account he demands from them a hearing; for unbelievers, not less than heathen nations, were utterly deaf to his voice. Now, although the people were so far from being in their unbroken strength, that the dispersion of them had left but a small number behind, yet God bids them consider how wonderfully they have been hitherto preserved, that they may not doubt that he will henceforth act towards them, as he has hitherto acted, the part of both father and mother.
